#10239. Why Your AI Agent Can't Read the Web (and How to Build a Fetch Layer That Can)

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

This is the least glamorous part of building with LLMs and it's where a lot of agent projects quietly fall over. The model is rarely the problem. The fetch is. In this article we'll look at why live web retrieval has become so unreliable for AI tools, what the numbers say about the shift, and how to build a small, well-behaved fetch layer in Python that fails loudly instead of feeding your model garbage.

A few years ago, a plain requests.get() worked on most of the public web. That's no longer true, and the reason is simple: there are now more bots than people.

According to the 2025 Imperva Bad Bot Report, automated traffic made up 51% of all web traffic in 2024. That's the first time in a decade it has passed human activity. Bad bots alone (scrapers, credential stuffers, scalpers) went from 32% to 37% of traffic in a single year.

Source: Imperva Bad Bot Report 2024 and 2025

From a site owner's point of view, your polite research agent and a credential-stuffing botnet look much the same at the network edge. Both are non-browser clients making fast requests from data-center IP ranges. So the defaults have tightened. In July 2025 Cloudflare began blocking known AI crawlers by default for new customers, and bot management products now look at TLS fingerprints, header order, IP reputation and JavaScript execution, not just the User-Agent string.

It helps to understand the publisher's side of the deal, because it explains why your agent is being treated with suspicion.

Cloudflare splits AI crawling into three purposes: training (collecting data to train models), search (building an index for AI search answers) and user action (fetching a page because a person just asked a question). Training dominates.

Training crawls take content and send nothing back. Cloudflare measures this with a crawl-to-referral ratio: how many pages a platform crawls for every visitor it sends to the site. In its crawl-to-click gap analysis, the ratios for some AI platforms ran into the tens of thousands, compared with single digits for traditional search.

If you ran a publication and saw those numbers, you'd block too. The catch is that blocking is usually done by user agent or IP range, so it hits user-action fetches as well. Those are the ones that happen when a person asks your agent to read a specific article, and Cloudflare's 2025 Year in Review found they grew more than 15x during the year. Your agent is caught in a fight it didn't start.

The mix of crawlers also shifts quickly, which makes static allow and block lists fragile on both sides:

And restrictions keep piling up. The Consent in Crisis study audited 14,000 web domains and found that a large and fast-growing share of the sources behind the C4 training corpus now restrict AI crawlers, either through robots.txt or their terms of service.

Source: Longpre et al., Consent in Crisis (NeurIPS 2024)

So that's the environment your agent fetches in. Here's how to build for it.

Before writing any retry logic, put names on your failures. "The request failed" is useless to both you and the model. In practice almost every failed fetch falls into one of four buckets:

Bucket 2 is the dangerous one, because a block page often comes back with a 200 OK. If you don't check, the model will happily summarise "Checking your browser before accessing..." as if it were the article.

Here's a compact fetch layer in Python using httpx and the standard library's robots.txt parser. It's around 100 lines and covers the four buckets above.

Use a descriptive user agent with a contact URL. It costs you nothing and site operators are far more likely to allow a client they can identify and reach. Then check robots.txt (standardised as RFC 9309) before every new host.

The lru_cache means you fetch robots.txt once per origin rather than once per page. In a long-running service you'll want a cache with a TTL instead, since robots.txt files do change.

This is the core of the layer. Instead of returning raw HTML, return a result that says which bucket you landed in.

The marker list is deliberately simple. It won't catch every interstitial, but it catches the common ones, and a false "blocked" is much cheaper than a confident summary of a CAPTCHA page. Log every blocked result with its first few hundred characters so you can grow the list from real data.

Retries should depend on the bucket. Throttled and broken responses get exponential backoff with jitter. Blocked and not-allowed responses get no retries at all.

Note the cap on wait. A site sending Retry-After: 3600 is telling you to go away for an hour. An interactive agent should report that to the user rather than block a request thread for that long.

The cheapest fetch is the one you don't make. Agents often re-read the same documentation page several times in one session. Store the ETag and Last-Modified headers and send them back as If-None-Match and If-Modified-Since. A 304 Not Modified response costs the server almost nothing and lowers the odds of being rate limited.

Wire these into fetch() by passing headers=conditional_headers(url) to client.get(). On a 304, return the cached text. On a 200, call remember().

Finally, don't hide failures from the LLM. Give the tool output a structured shape so the model can reason about it:

(extract_main_text is whatever readability or boilerplate-removal step you already use. Libraries like trafilatura work well here.)

With this in place, the model's answer changes from a made-up summary to "I couldn't read that page because the site blocks automated access. Here's what I found from two other sources." That's a better product, and it builds trust with users.

Once you've done everything above, some legitimate user-action fetches will still fail. That's usually because the site blocks data-center IP ranges outright, not because of anything your agent did. Teams handle this in a few ways, roughly in order of preference:

The principle is the same in every case: the network path is a reliability decision, not a way around a site's wishes. Your robots.txt check and your honest user agent should stay in place whichever route the request takes.

Once your fetch layer returns structured results, observability is easy. Emit one event per fetch with the host, status bucket and latency, and watch these:

If you're prototyping agents with AI coding assistants, ask them to generate these metrics hooks from the start. They're easy to bolt on now and painful to add later. For a sense of how well current tools handle this kind of infrastructure code, Vibe Coder Journal publishes hands-on reviews and benchmarks of AI coding tools.

The web your agent reads in 2026 isn't the open, fetch-anything web many of us learned on. More than half the traffic is automated, publishers have good reasons to be wary of AI crawlers, and the defaults now lean toward blocking. You can't change that. You can make your agent a good citizen, though: one that identifies itself, respects the rules, backs off when asked, and tells the truth when it can't read something.

Most of the reliability gains come from the unglamorous parts: classifying failures, caching and passing honest errors to the model. Get those right and your agent will feel much more dependable, even on the days when half the web won't let it in.

It depends on the jurisdiction, the site's terms of service and what you do with the content. Respecting robots.txt and site terms is the baseline. For commercial products, get proper legal advice.

Many site owners expect it to, and RFC 9309 makes no exception for user-triggered fetches. The safest default is to obey it and tell the user when a page is disallowed.

Many bot-protection systems serve a challenge page with a 200 status. Check the body for challenge markers before passing it to the model, as in the looks_blocked() function above.

Only for pages that render their main content with JavaScript. Try a plain HTTP fetch first. Headless browsers are slower, cost more to run and are easier to fingerprint.

#10238. MicroLighter: Syntax Highlighter

Here we go! Syntax highlighting for code blocks without the complicated markup, spans, classes, and bloated JavaScript, courtesy of Uncle Dave.

MicroLighter is pretty much straight-up CSS leaning on Custom Highlights, using the ::highlight() pseudo… which is Baseline this year!

It accomplishes exactly every we need around here at CSS-Tricks — themes, line numbers, multiple language support, semantic markup, etc. — but without the added dependencies we rely on.

Chris made a custom WordPress block years and years ago that plugs in Prism.js. There’s certainly nothing wrong with Prism. It’s robust, supports a crap-ton of languages, is also super lightweight, and plenty battled-tested. Either way, I’ll certainly be looking at integrating this into our WordPress block.

It’s not that there isn’t any JavaScript involved. It’s that less of it is needed. And it leans so hard into modern CSS that it brings things like light-dark() support and custom properties along for the ride, meaning rolling your own theme is totally doable.

Plus, it’s super modular in the sense that you can snag the things you want à la carte: specific themes, just the languages you need to support, line numbers, a web component.

Reminds me too of this clever little web font that brings syntax highlighting along for the ride. I’ve been happily using that on my personal site for a while without any fuss.

Update (August 31, 2026): I just finished adding MicroLighter to this site in place of Prism. I haven’t benchmarked performance in terms of page speed, etc., but I can say that the savings is pretty significant. Where Prism came in at 35 KB raw (9.3 KB gzipped), MicroLighter is at 13.9 KB raw (5.2 KB gzipped). Not bad at all considering there are WordPress-specific customizations that had to be baked in.

Syntax highlighting for code blocks without the […] bloated JavaScript

This is an unreasonable claim, even for CSS-Tricks. Have you looked at how much weight Prism.js adds? Its scripting accounts for around 23,776 bytes of https://css-tricks.com/wp-content/themes/CSS-Tricks-19/js/min/global-concat.min.js, under 8KB gzipped. I’m actually not even certain that MicroLighter is smaller, once you include roughly the same set of languages; they’re pretty similar. If you use its touted lazy loading of grammars, it will certainly be slower.

There are, and have always been, good options that require no JavaScript; whereas this one fundamentally requires it (Custom Highlights are DOM-only, no serialisation defined or in my opinion likely to ever be defined).

Another limitation of this approach, which I reckon is important to mention, is that you are very limited in what you can style: simplifying slightly, it’s just color, background-color, text-decoration and text-shadow.

It’s very common to use font-weight: bold or font-style: italic in syntax highlighting. You can’t do that with this approach.

Well, like I said, it checks the boxes of what I’m looking for in a tool like this. It’s not that there aren’t alternatives that pack in much more features, again, like I said. I’m more interested in that MicroLighter doesn’t even touch the DOM.

#10236. Streaming comes to API Gateway: real-time and AI-ready APIs, without changing your spec

For most of the last decade, an API call looked like a transaction. A client sent a request, waited, and got a complete response back in one piece. That model is exactly what most API management tooling — including API Gateway — was built to handle, and it still describes a huge amount of production traffic.

But that no longer describes all traffic types. A model generating a response emits tokens as it produces them, not in one batch at the end. An agent working through a multi-step task reports progress as it goes. A dashboard, a collaborative editor, a live inference endpoint — these all need a connection that stays open and carries data in both directions.

Until now, developers building those experiences in API Gateway had to make an uncomfortable choice: put API Gateway in front of their APIs and give up streaming, or route streaming endpoints around the gateway and give up the authentication, API key enforcement, and observability that made the gateway essential in the first place. Teams ended up with a split estate — governed APIs on one path, ungoverned streaming traffic on another.

We're announcing that streaming support in API Gateway is available in Public Preview. Your streaming endpoints can now sit behind the same gateway, with the same policies, as everything else you serve.

For AI applications, streaming also strengthens API Gateway's connection to Gemini platform. A gateway that uses model routing now streams responses from Gemini, Claude and OpenAI gpt-oss models in model garden in Gemini platform as they're generated, and streaming backends you host anywhere else work the same way. Alongside Apigee and Agent Gateway in Gemini platform, API Gateway is the lightweight entry point to Google Cloud's AI gateway capabilities.

API Gateway now supports the full range of streaming patterns modern APIs rely on:

Streams can stay open for up to one hour. As with any long-lived connection, clients should implement reconnection logic so that a session survives the end of a stream — a well-behaved WebSocket or SSE client should be doing this anyway.

This is the part we are most pleased with: there is nothing new to learn.

Streaming is not a different product, a different resource type, or a different way of describing your API. There are no new extensions to add, no streaming-specific annotations, no separate spec for streaming operations. The same document that describes your existing API describes your streaming API.

Everything you already rely on continues to work exactly as before:

During Public Preview, you opt-in when creating the gateway:

That single flag is the entire difference. At GA, it is planned that streaming will simply be how API Gateway behaves, with no opt-in required and, as during Preview, no changes to your API config.

Alongside streaming, gateways get a deterministic default hostname:

Previously the default gateway.dev hostname included a generated hash, which meant you could not know your gateway's URL until after you had created it. That is a small thing that causes a lot of friction: you can't write the endpoint into a client config, a Terraform module, a CI pipeline, a firewall allowlist, or a partner integration doc until the resource exists — and if you tear the environment down and rebuild it, the URL changes underneath you.

Now the hostname is a pure function of values you already chose. You can generate it, template it, document it, and commit it to source control before the gateway exists, and you get the same URL every time you rebuild the same gateway in the same project and region. For anyone managing environments as code, or promoting a configuration from dev to staging to prod, this removes an entire category of bootstrapping problem.

Streaming isn't a niche feature for AI applications — it's the expected interaction pattern.

Users expect to see a model's response appear as it's generated, not after a thirty-second pause. Agents need to report intermediate steps. Tool-calling protocols and remote MCP servers depend on long-lived, incrementally-delivered connections. An API management layer that can't stream severely limits the user experience of AI applications.

With streaming, API Gateway becomes a viable front door for that agentic traffic — and the value of a front door is exactly the same as it's always been, only more urgent. AI endpoints are expensive, they consume quota, they need per-consumer authentication and rate limiting, and they need to be observable. These are the governance problems that an AI gateway is intended to solve. The alternative — every team standing up its own proxy in front of its own model endpoint — is how organizations end up unable to answer basic questions about who is calling what.

Model routing in API Gateway lets you expose a single OpenAI-compatible endpoint and dispatch requests to Gemini, Claude, or OpenAI gpt-oss models based on the model field in the request payload. Model routing plus streaming means clients get a familiar, standards-based streaming interface, while you retain centralized control over which models are reachable, by whom, and under what policy.

Streaming, model routing and MCP support are all features within API Gateway that provide a lightweight on-ramp to AI gateway capabilities within Google Cloud. These AI gateway capabilities allow teams to monitor, secure and control agentic traffic of tools, models and agents in their ecosystem, and they're delivered as a composable suite so you can choose the right gateway for each use case. For more expansive AI policies and full lifecycle management, use Apigee. To manage and secure agent connectivity, use Agent Gateway in Gemini platform. You can also combine these gateways: API Gateway or Apigee can sit in front of your agents and APIs, or behind Agent Gateway so your agents can reach models, tools, and MCP servers. For example, you can route your agent's egress through Agent Gateway for strict security governance, and then pass the request to API Gateway to handle model routing.

A few things to plan around while the feature is in Preview:

If you're already using API Gateway, the fastest way to see this working is to point a new streaming-enabled gateway at an existing backend that emits SSE and watch the events arrive incrementally. No spec changes needed.

#10235. animation-trigger

Experimental: Check browser support before using this in production.

The CSS animation-trigger property delays the start of a CSS animation until a specific trigger occurs. More specifically, it listens for a named trigger and controls how the animation plays or pauses in response.

This behavior has traditionally been JavaScript territory, typically with the Intersection Observer API.

Scroll-triggered animations should not be confused with scroll-driven animations. Although both rely on scroll or view timelines, they are fundamentally different concepts. We’ll get to those differences in a minute.

The animation-trigger property is defined in the Animation Triggers specification

The property accepts none, or a comma-separated list of triggers and their corresponding actions:

The “trigger” in animation-trigger can refer to either timeline-based triggers, such as scroll or view progress timelines, or event-based triggers like DOM events (e.g., a click). In this entry, we’ll mainly focus on timeline triggers. If you’re curious about event-based triggers, you can check out the official spec.

By default, trigger names have a global scope. If multiple elements define the same trigger name, the element that comes later in the cascade gets chosen. You can restrict the scope of a trigger to a specific DOM subtree with the trigger-scope property.

Some actions aren’t  or  only, meaning it’s possible to play-backwards when entering and play-forwards when exiting.

To actually use animation-trigger, you’ll typically need to set up a timeline trigger first. That controls when an animation starts based on where an element is within a timeline (like scroll or viewport position). More specifically, it activates when the element enters a defined activation range within that timeline.

To set up your timeline trigger, you’ll first define a custom  (like --fade-in) to link it to your animation-trigger , followed by a  timeline like a view() or scroll() function.

Then, you specify the  (such as contain) to dictate exactly when the trigger turns “on” inside the viewport.

You can also provide an optional  to define the outer boundary where the trigger stays active before turning “off”, though if you leave it out, the browser just defaults to your activation range.

To get a better feel for how this works, check out the timeline ranges visualizer from the Chrome team.

If you use different ranges, the active range must include the activation range; otherwise, the trigger can’t turn “on.”

While you can use all the individual longhand properties:

…you’ll almost always want to use the shorthand instead:

Unlike many CSS shorthands (like background or border), the order of values matters here, so you can’t rearrange them freely.

It’s worth noting that triggers and animations don’t have to be on the same element. You can define the timeline-trigger on a parent and apply the animation-trigger to multiple child elements. When the parent enters view, all children can animate together.

Let’s create a simple text reveal animation. We’ll use an element as the trigger point. Once you scroll past it, the animation plays and the text fades in.

First, define a timeline trigger on the trigger element:

This sets up a trigger named --trigger that activates based on scroll position. The range contain / cover means the animation is triggered when the element is fully visible in the scrollport (contain) and continues to run as long as any part of it remains visible in the scrollport (cover).

Next, we’ll apply the animation-trigger to the text you want to animate, along with the animation itself:

The cool part is that you can mix and match different animation-action values to get very different behaviors using the same trigger. Here’s a quick demo showing the same setup with different animation actions:

With scroll-driven animations, the animation’s progress is directly tied to scroll position. As you scroll, the animation scrubs forward or backward in sync with the timeline. There’s no concept of a “start” or “fire” moment.

In contrast, scroll-triggered animations are state-based rather than continuous. A trigger has a binary state and when a condition is met—such as an element entering a defined range—the trigger fires an associated action (like play, pause, or reset). Once triggered, the animation behaves like your regular CSS animations with no link to the scroll progress.

Here’s a pretty cool demo to see the differences between the two, courtesy of utlitybend:

The animation-trigger property is defined in the Animation Triggers specification, which is currently in Editor’s Drafts. That means the information can change between now and what it becomes an official Candidate Recommendation.

#10234. Microsoft's moolah mountain is more massive than ever. It just doesn't want the people who built it

Capitalism can seem so perverse. Take Microsoft, which is celebrating record financial performance by inviting 60,000 employees to consider continuing their careers outside the company. Voluntary redundancy may seem to make sense when a company's running out of cash, but Microsoft is dripping with the stuff.

Redmond's first quarter for fiscal 2027 was a bonanza for the tech giant. Its Azure business is up over 48 percent y-o-y, revenues are through the roof, and it has so much moolah it returned $10.2 billion to shareholders in the form of dividends and share repurchases.

This latter move probably soothed CEO Satya Nadella, who recently suffered, due to the vagaries of C-suite reimbursement and incentive packages, a 6 percent cut in his pocket money. But as he’s also a stockholder with about 0.01 percent of the company, his share of the cash return presumably eased the pain.

He won't have been offered redundo. Jenkins, the large wheelbarrow if you please.

Microsoft, then, can afford all its employees, each of whom contributed about $1.5 million to SatNad's bottom line in the last full fiscal year. The "massive efficiencies and RoI of AI" make a great line for a company flogging magic LLM juice, but the evidence remains elusive. AI is, of course, still the reason. Nothing else matters these days. It's just that it's not today's AI.

Among all the fulsome figures it put on display for Q1 2027, analysts noted that Microsoft's capital expenditure wasn't as spendy as expected. Quite a lot has been pushed into next calendar year, not because it's not there to be spent – Microsoft could build a 1:1 scale model of the Vatican filled with robot priests if it wanted – but because so much it wanted to mash the Buy Now button for was "Out of stock. More expected soon."

This is bad. MS added 88 datacenters in its most recent full financial year: fiscal 2026. That’s not enough datacenters for a cloud business expected to grow by half again in 2027, and hugely not enough to do the other thing. Lags in the cadence of deforestation, dewatering and detonation of the planet can't be tolerated. Thus there are contracts signed to get things back on track PDQ, with mucho, mucho, mucho sponduiks.

In its most recent Q1 earnings call, Microsoft is hinting, those selfsame analysts say, that it will have to go to the debt market and go into "negative free cash flow" territory in 2028. In other words, as well as spending its own bank, the company will be taking out massive loans.

This is why Billy and Bhavya Dev have to go. The cost of borrowing depends on the financial health of the borrower, and that boils down to how much profit you're making from the money you earn. A big round of redundancies, which are very costly in themselves, sits on the books of the year they happen. The hole in expenditure left by the vanished salaries lives on. The capital must flow.

Will this work? Last week, we listed the reasons why it might not — price competition between rivals and increasingly powerful local and open weight models, supply side shortages, you know the litany by now. This week is Groundhog week, with fresh stories singing the same songs from different choirs.

Any sensible soul, especially developers sitting on the sharp end of AI's forcible insertion into their working lives, will know how uncertain the job market is. Voluntary redundancy is a very high stakes bet, and the game is very different if you're in an organization that's going downhill and may need to get rid of you later with far less cash available than if you're nominally making $1.5 million in a place whose biggest problem is that it physically can't move into a bigger shell.

On average, only 5 percent or so of those offered voluntary redundancy take it, which Microsoft HR will have factored in. It's cold outside and snug within, so that may be on the high side. The biggest knock-on of such schemes is cultural, with only the very confident moving on out, a disproportionate loss of talent and role models. Hey, the cost of doing business, right?

For those who do decide to leave and watch the fireworks from outside the tent, part of the deal is career development resources. Sounds great, if anyone knows what technical careers will look like if either AI works and does indeed do all the work, or it fails and the global financial system throws a humongous wobble. Or anything in between.

So, here's an exercise in very dark humor quite fitting for the Halloween season. Ask your favorite AI what careers will be available for coders made redundant by AI. It will give you a long and plausible list. Then ask it – and yourself – why AI won't be able to do any of those jobs too. Buying a truck and a wrench and calling yourself a plumber is probably safest. Nobody will ever want AI to fix their toilet.  ®

#10230. Vintage fun: Prodding AI agents using retro hardware just because you can

'It helps me stretch what I can do in the current age of AI coding, and keeps my curiosity alive'

From the department of "pointless but still cool" comes word of some kit being repurposed as a terminal for AI agents.

AWS developer advocate Darko Mesaroš has connected a teletype to a modern command-line interface to revel in the delight of interacting with today's AI technology via a combination of a DECwriter and fanfold paper, or the display and keyboard of a computer whose heyday ended 40 years ago.

Mesaroš' project involved AWS Kiro, a Command Line Interface (CLI) and agentic coding service. We would, however, contend that this is more about seeing what retro hardware can be made to do.

Two problems needed solving: getting data to and from the teletype, and formatting the output to work on a piece of kit from another era of computing. He used Hayes modem emulation to deal with the serial connection, and Agent Client Protocol (ACP) for working with Kiro.

Mesaroš used a WiModem232 for the former. The device emulates a standard Hayes-compatible modem and, according to Mesaroš, "Folks initially used this to connect Commodore 64s to BBSes in the modern era" (he started his computing journey with a Commodore 64). The latter, getting the Kiro CLI to work on a Teletype, was a little more complicated. Kiro's CLI isn't really suitable for a teleprinter capable of 30 characters per second, after all.

A simple Rust application took Kiro's output (obtained via ACP) and turned it into something that a teletype, or dumb terminal, could handle.

As we said, seemingly pointless, but making it work required knowledge of Rust, competence with containers, an understanding of ACP, and more than a little creative thinking. So, while one might argue it is pointless from a technical perspective, it is wonderfully educational otherwise.

The repository is available and focuses on Kiro for obvious reasons (Mesaroš is an AWS developer advocate after all), but in a chat with The Register, Mesaroš said the concept was portable. He said, "Any coding assistant or any harness that supports ACP, this should work, right? I built it for Kiro, but it uses the standard ACP protocol, so I could easily plug in Claude Code or Codex. Anything that basically can serve as an ACP server should be perfectly fine.

There might be some issues. "The biggest problem with this thing is that it doesn't really handle packet drops at all," he explained. "Like, if you drop packets, they're just gone. There're no retries. It's just spitting information out."

And then there is buffering. Or the lack of it. Mesaroš said, "There's actually no buffering happening here. Literally, it just comes down through the fire hose through this serial device, and the bottleneck itself is the serial device."

Mesaroš had toyed with using the GPIO pins on a Raspberry Pi, but settled on the serial device instead, since everything worked "out of the box." "It's kind of cheating," he admitted, "but it's also kind of good."

Mesaroš collects vintage hardware, with a stash that ranges from home computers made by Commodore and Sinclair,  to a 1974 Data General Eclipse minicomputer and a plethora of Sun hardware. And, of course, an old Decwriter. He is also a dab hand with the soldering iron, having learned the skills to keep old hardware operational. Unlike today's equipment. "I have this big peeve over modern computers, where you just can't fix them," he said, "and it feels like such a waste of resources that when my MacBook dies I just have to drill a hole through it so nobody steals my data, and throw it away."

As for Kiro-TTY – or accessing a coding assistant or agent over serial using a decades-old device – he wrote on his blog, "This absolutely serves no purpose."

However, it did provide a novel way of working out how the ACP protocol worked. Perhaps not so usefully, it also taught the developer how to debug serial connectivity.

"And in general it helps me stretch what I can do in the current age of AI coding, and keeps my curiosity alive."

The destination might be pointless from a modern perspective, but the journey getting there is anything but. ®

#10229. Creating Web Widgets Using the Document Picture-in-Picture API

Firefox 151 recently shipped the Document Picture-in-Picture API. This isn’t the same thing as the (regular?) Picture-in-Picture API, which pushes videos into a resizable window that remains visible even after switching browser tabs or OS windows. No, the Document Picture-in-Picture API enables us to put anything into the window.

I guess we can think of these windows as web widgets. We can use them for floating stock tickers, live chat conversations, playlists, to-do lists, notes, spreadsheets — anything that we’d want to keep on the screen at all times.

The general idea is that we create a Document Picture-in-Picture window (DPIP window), and then we put HTML, CSS, and JavaScript into it. It’s pretty simple when you think about it, but as we explore how the Document Picture-in-Picture API works, we’re going to tackle a slightly more complex scenario that you’ll probably run into.

We’re going to clone a stock ticker from the main document into a DPIP window. This not only gives us an opportunity to talk about some relevant media queries and pseudo-classes, which we’ll use to write targeted CSS for the DPIP window, but it’s also a stark reminder that taking a HTML component out of context can break the CSS, so you’ll need to keep that in mind.

But for it to work, you’ll need to open the demo in debug mode. This is because picture-in-picture doesn’t work in nested browsing contexts such as CodePen
